summary:
Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, governs legal gender recognition. Article 43 lets any person aged 16 or over apply directly to the Civil Registry to change the gender mention on their own entry, by declaration, with no diagnosis and no period of medical treatment; Human Rights Watch recorded the end of the previous dysphoria-diagnosis and two-year treatment requirements when parliament passed the law. Recognition is open from age 12 under conditions set in the statute, which also regulates consent to medical procedures for minors between 12 and 16.

Bias motive is an aggravating factor in criminal law, not a stand-alone offence. A Spanish criminal-law analysis notes that gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code: the hate-speech aggravation in Article 22.4 and the penalties in Article 510 (one to four years plus a fine of six to twelve months) come from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 reformed offences against sexual freedom in Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. Threats or violence against a trans person are prosecuted as threats, injury or coercion, with the bias motive attached to that charge.

Courts have begun attaching the aggravator. In July 2026 a court in Vigo applied the transphobia aggravating circumstance for the first time at first-instance level, in a case of WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman; the defendant was fined EUR 300. In Valencia a group harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them; the only adult defendant was sentenced to six months' imprisonment and two minors were dealt with separately.

Facility access follows legal gender self-determination rather than a birth-sex rule, and no blanket statutory bar stops a trans person using the facilities of their gender. Coverage contrasts this with the United Kingdom, where the Equality and Human Rights Commission's statutory code moves toward stricter single-sex provision applied case by case.

Marriage and joint adoption have been open to same-sex couples since 2005, and Ley 4/2023 extends parental recognition to unmarried couples, including couples the statute classes as same-sex. Legal change of gender has not required surgery or sterilisation.

The 2023 statute also bans non-consensual normalising surgery on intersex children, adds anti-discrimination measures in healthcare, employment and housing, expands assisted reproduction and strengthens sexuality education.

Official and commercial assessments are uniformly positive. UK consular travel advice describes Spain as a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers with active communities and venues; a travel operator's country guide rates it safe and welcoming, naming Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia as the strongest hubs while noting more conservative attitudes outside the large cities. The national tourism institute lists eight flagship destinations (Madrid's Chueca district, Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Cadiz, the Canary Islands, Sitges and Torremolinos) and a Destinations for Diversity certification for destinations and venues meeting its open, discrimination-free standard.

Survey evidence is dated but consistent. In a 2016 survey of 23 countries Spain ranked the most trans-supportive, the only country where a majority backed unrestricted change of legal gender designation, with restroom access support above 70 percent and a quarter of respondents saying they knew a trans person. A 2013 Pew poll recorded 88 percent acceptance, the highest of the 39 countries surveyed.

Protection is not uniform across the country. In 2023 the incoming regional government of Madrid repealed the region's non-discrimination law, repealed its conversion-therapy ban as it applies to trans people, removed the penalties attached to conversion therapy and repealed several regional trans legal recognitions. The national statute remains in force there; the regional layer of protection does not.
tangentialFactors:
Spain sits with Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay among the countries that moved to self-identification by administrative process, the comparison Human Rights Watch used when the law passed.

The historical record is one of state persecution. Under the Franco dictatorship (1936-1975) thousands of gay men and women were jailed, held in camps or confined to mental institutions, some in special prisons for detainees classed as homosexual, and vagrancy laws were applied to suspected dissidents on the basis of actual or perceived homosexuality. Trans people were prosecuted under public scandal offences and municipal ordinances until the end of the 1980s. In 2013 the interior minister said same-sex marriage endangered the survival of the human species and opposed equal legal protection for such marriages.

Reporting on anti-LGBT violence is inconsistent between monitors, which limits what any single figure shows. The Secretary of State for Security reported a 4 percent decrease in 2018, while the Observatorio Madrileño recorded a 7 percent increase and Catalonia's Observatori contra l'Homofòbia a 30 percent increase in early 2019. None of the three publishes a denominator alongside the change.

Residents apply at the Civil Registry directly under Article 43 of Ley 4/2023: a declaration by the applicant aged 16 or over, with no diagnosis, no treatment period and no surgery or sterilisation requirement. Applicants aged 12 to 16 proceed under the conditions in the statute, which also fixes when their own consent governs medical procedures.

The same law bans non-consensual normalising surgery on intersex children, extends assisted reproduction, provides parental recognition for unmarried couples including those the statute classes as same-sex, and adds anti-discrimination protection in healthcare, employment and housing.

Regional protection varies and residents should not assume the regional layer matches the national one. Madrid's regional government repealed its non-discrimination law in 2023, repealed the conversion-therapy ban as it applies to trans people, removed the penalties for conversion therapy and repealed several regional trans legal recognitions.
outOfScopeNotes:
Gender expression has no free-standing hate-crime offence in the Criminal Code; protection depends on the bias aggravator being attached to an underlying offence, and the Vigo ruling is a first-instance decision rather than appellate authority.

No consolidated national dataset of prosecutions or convictions for gender-identity bias crimes was located in the sources reviewed, and the available trend figures conflict between the national security ministry and regional monitors.

The attitude data cited here dates from 2013 and 2016 and predates Ley 4/2023; no post-2023 national survey was found in the sources reviewed.

The scope of the Madrid regional repeals, in particular which regional trans legal recognitions were withdrawn, is not detailed in the sources reviewed.
